High Sabbath
HIGH SAB-bath
n. phrase
High + Sabbath; the KJV phrase at John 19:31 (that sabbath day was an high day) for a Sabbath that coincided with one of the annual feast-days, making it doubly sacred; Greek megalē hēmera, “great day.”

Biblical Definition

The high Sabbath in biblical usage is a Sabbath that coincides with one of the annual feast-days, making it a doubly-sacred day in the Jewish calendar. The phrase appears explicitly in John 19:31 of the Sabbath following Christ’s crucifixion: the Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away. The Sabbath following Christ’s death was a high Sabbath because it fell during Passover week—specifically, it was the Sabbath of the Feast of Unleavened Bread (the first day of which, Nisan 15, was itself a high-day Sabbath, regardless of which day of the week it fell on; the regular weekly Sabbath that year coincided with the feast-week, doubling the sanctity of the day). Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the categorical distinction. OT Israel had two kinds of Sabbaths: the weekly Sabbath (every seventh day, regardless of season) and the annual feast-day Sabbaths (the first day of Unleavened Bread, the day after the Passover Sabbath, the Feast of Weeks/Pentecost, the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, the first day of Tabernacles, and the eighth day of Tabernacles—each of these annual feast-days was itself a Sabbath in the sense of being a day of cessation from ordinary work and holy convocation, but not necessarily falling on the seventh day of the week). The annual Sabbaths could land on any day of the week, and when one of them coincided with the weekly seventh-day Sabbath, the day was doubly sacred: a high Sabbath. Second, the chronological significance for Christ’s death. The high Sabbath of John 19:31 has implications for the chronology of the crucifixion-and-resurrection. Many traditional readings have held that Christ was crucified on Friday and rose on Sunday; some careful chronological readings have argued that the high Sabbath of John 19:31 indicates a Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion (with the high Sabbath being the annual Sabbath of the first day of Unleavened Bread, not the weekly Saturday), allowing for the three-days-and-three-nights of Matt 12:40. The chronological details are contested, but the recognition of high Sabbaths as a category distinct from weekly Sabbaths is structurally important for the reading. Third, the broader typological substance. The high Sabbath as a doubly-sacred day—weekly Sabbath plus annual feast-Sabbath—points to the consummate sacred-time of the new heavens and earth, where the rest of the eternal Sabbath is also the rest of the consummated feast (the marriage supper of the Lamb, the gathering in the heavenly city) in one perpetual high-Sabbath that brings both rhythms together forever. The categorical distinction between weekly and annual Sabbaths therefore matters not only chronologically but theologically: the New Covenant believer’s ultimate rest is the consummate high Sabbath where the weekly and annual rhythms meet in eternal worship of the Lord at His feast.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 treats SABBATH as the day of rest; the high Sabbath of John 19:31 is the doubly-sacred Sabbath that coincides with an annual feast-day, making the day doubly holy in the Jewish calendar.

HIGH SABBATH — A Sabbath day that coincides with one of the annual feast-days of the Jewish calendar, making it doubly sacred. For that sabbath day was an high day (John 19:31).

FEAST-DAY, n. — A day appointed for some particular religious celebration; in OT Israel, the annual feast-days (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, etc.), each of which had its own appointed Sabbath of rest, distinct from the weekly seventh-day Sabbath.

Key Scripture

John 19:31 — "The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation, that the bodies should not remain upon the cross on the sabbath day, (for that sabbath day was an high day,) besought Pilate that their legs might be broken, and that they might be taken away."

Leviticus 23:7-8 — "In the first day ye shall have an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein. But ye shall offer an offering made by fire unto the LORD seven days: in the seventh day is an holy convocation: ye shall do no servile work therein."

Matthew 12:40 — "For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale’s belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth."

Revelation 19:9 — "And he saith unto me, Write, Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb. And he saith unto me, These are the true sayings of God."

Modern Corruption

The high-Sabbath doctrine is corrupted chiefly by the general loss of the categorical distinction between weekly and annual Sabbaths, which produces confused readings of the crucifixion chronology (forcing all Sabbath-references in John 19 onto the weekly seventh-day Sabbath when the high Sabbath was actually the annual feast-day Sabbath)—and by the consequent loss of the typological richness of the consummate high Sabbath of the new heavens and earth.

expand to see more

The general loss of the categorical distinction between weekly and annual Sabbaths is the broader corruption that affects the high-Sabbath doctrine. Contemporary readers, accustomed to thinking of the Sabbath as exclusively the weekly seventh-day Sabbath, force every Sabbath-reference in the Gospels onto the weekly Saturday, missing the annual feast-day Sabbaths that the OT explicitly establishes (Lev 23) and that the Jewish first-century calendar uniformly preserved. The high Sabbath of John 19:31 is one specific example: a Sabbath that was an high day precisely because an annual feast-Sabbath coincided with the weekly Sabbath (or because the annual feast-Sabbath was itself the day in question, depending on the chronological reading). The recovery is the recovery of the categorical distinction: OT and first-century Jewish Sabbaths included both weekly seventh-day and annual feast-day, and the careful reading of the Gospels’ chronology requires attention to which kind was operative in any given passage.

The typological substance of the high Sabbath as a doubly-sacred day points toward the consummate sacred-time of the new heavens and earth, where the weekly-Sabbath-rhythm of God’s ordered worship and the annual-feast-rhythm of the redemptive-historical celebrations meet in one perpetual eternal-Sabbath that is also the consummated wedding-feast of the Lamb. The loss of this typological substance is part of the broader loss of OT festal typology that has impoverished contemporary preaching. The recovery restores not only the chronological precision (for example, the careful reading of the resurrection-week sequence) but also the doctrinal-and-pastoral substance: the saint’s ultimate rest is the consummate high Sabbath of eternal worship at the marriage supper of the Lamb in the new heavens and earth, where every weekly Lord’s Day and every annual gospel-commemoration finds its substantive eschatological fulfillment in one perpetual high day before the throne.

Hebrew Roots

Greek megalē hēmera (great day—John 19:31’s explicit phrase); the doubly-sacred Sabbath that coincides with an annual feast-day in the Jewish calendar; chronologically significant for the crucifixion-resurrection sequence and typologically pointing toward the consummate high Sabbath of the new heavens and earth where weekly and annual rhythms meet in eternal worship.

expand to see more

Greek megalē hēmera — great day, high day (John 19:31).

Hebrew shabbāt shabbātōn — a sabbath of sabbaths, a high Sabbath (used of Day of Atonement in Lev 16:31; 23:32 and Yom Kippur).

Hebrew miqra qodesh — holy convocation (the technical term for the annual feast-day Sabbaths in Lev 23).

Greek kuriakē hēmera — Lord’s Day (Rev 1:10; the Christian weekly day-of-worship).

Usage

"That sabbath day was an high day—John 19:31 distinguishes the high Sabbath of the crucifixion week from the ordinary weekly Sabbath."

"OT Israel had both weekly seventh-day Sabbaths and annual feast-day Sabbaths; when the two coincided, the day was a high Sabbath, doubly sacred."

"Loss of the categorical distinction produces confused chronological readings; recovery restores both the precise chronology and the typological substance of the consummate high Sabbath of the new heavens and earth."
